passage:
Subject: Cash plan, please poke holes

Hi Rekha,

I redid the plan for the studio this weekend. Nearly every invoice we have sent has been paid two or three months late, so I stopped believing the dates on them. In the new sheet, income arrives a quarter after the promise, whatever the client says. Rent, salaries and tools are paid out of that slower pace. On top of that, a separate account holds a cushion of two months' costs, and I am not allowed to count it as income. It looks gloomier on paper, but I slept better. If a client pays early, it becomes a bonus, not a rescue. Can you check my assumptions on Thursday?

Santosh

qa.q: How large a cushion did Santosh set aside in a separate account?
qa.a: Santosh set aside a cushion of two months' costs.

qa.q: What does Santosh's remark about sleeping better suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Santosh feels relieved and calmer, since the plan no longer depends on hoped-for payment dates.

qa.q: What other approach could help with late payments?
qa.a: Santosh could ask clients for part of the payment upfront or agree shorter payment terms, which brings cash in earlier.

qa.q: How might Rekha see the plan?
qa.a: Rekha may find it cautious but reassuring, and probably wants to test the assumptions before trusting it.

grounding: Santosh plans expenses as if income arrives a quarter later than promised and keeps a two-month cushion apart.

subtype: Approach: buffer and slack planning for late payments [Thinking]
passage:
Vidya, people ask why my agency survived year one when two of my friends' didn't. Honestly? I'm Eshaan, and I'm a pessimist about invoices. Before I spent a rupee, I asked myself: when do clients here actually pay? Not what the contract says. What really happens. My old boss used to wait sixty, sometimes ninety days. So I built my plan as if every invoice arrives a full quarter after the due date. If a client promises April, my sheet says July.
Then, on top of that, I kept two months of costs in a separate account that I don't touch. Not for growth, not for a new laptop. Pure reserve.
In month five, our biggest client paid eighty-three days late. My friends would have missed salaries. We just waited. It was boring, Vidya. Boring is exactly what I wanted.

qa.q: How many days late did the biggest client pay?
Why does Eshaan say boring was exactly what was wanted?
qa.a: Eshaan felt calm, even relieved, when the late payment came, because the plan had expected it; the lack of panic was the goal.

qa.q: What else could strengthen Eshaan's plan?
qa.a: Eshaan could agree clear payment terms and polite reminder dates with clients, while still keeping the reserve.

qa.q: How might the agency's staff have experienced the late payment?
qa.a: They got their salaries on time and may never have noticed the delay, unlike staff at the friends' agencies.

grounding: It shows a founder planning as if client money arrives a quarter late and keeping two months of reserve, reasoning from how late clients really pay.

Francis runs a small app studio from the desk next to mine in the co-working space, and I've watched how he plans. When he won his first government contract in March, most of us would have celebrated with new chairs. Francis wrote two columns on the glass wall, "Invoice date" and "Real date", and pushed every payment ninety days to the right. He told me, "Clients here pay late. If I plan on the invoice date, I'll be borrowing by July." Then he moved some money to another account and stuck a note on his screen: "Two months. Do not touch."
I don't know if he slept better. But when the ministry's payment got stuck until September, he didn't let anyone go. He just stopped buying biscuits for the pantry for a while.
— Sharmila

qa.q: What did the note on Francis's screen say?
What does Francis's planning suggest about how he felt about the contract?
qa.a: He seems cautious and a bit wary, glad of the contract but worried about running short if payment came late; Sharmila can't know for sure.

qa.q: What else could Francis do while waiting for the stuck payment?
qa.a: He could follow up politely with the ministry on a set schedule and look for smaller clients who pay faster.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see Francis's approach compared with the others?
qa.a: Sharmila sees it as more careful: the others would have bought new chairs, but his plan kept everyone employed when the payment stuck.

grounding: It shows a founder shifting every expected payment ninety days later and keeping two months of reserve, because clients often pay late.
